facts.claim: The GoodWork framework evaluates work through excellence, ethics, and engagement.
facts.mechanism: Because High-quality performance, responsibility to others, and personal meaning can diverge, so all three must be examined.
facts.commonError: Good work means only being highly skilled at a task.
facts.whyWrong: Technical excellence without ethical responsibility or engagement is incomplete in the framework.

facts.claim: Good Work by Gardner, Csikszentmihalyi, and Damon was published in 2001.
facts.mechanism: Because The book synthesized interview research on professionals and the institutions shaping their practice.
facts.commonError: The GoodWork Project was a survey of leisure happiness.
facts.whyWrong: Its central subject was professional work at the intersection of excellence and ethics.

facts.claim: Vital engagement combines flow with subjective meaning in a sustained relationship to an activity.
facts.mechanism: Because Absorption supplies immediate involvement while valued identity and purpose make the activity matter across time.
facts.commonError: Any enjoyable flow episode is automatically a calling.
facts.whyWrong: Vital engagement requires enduring significance in addition to temporary absorption.

facts.claim: Vital engagement typically develops through repeated interaction between a person and a valued domain.
facts.mechanism: Because Practice increases skill, the domain supplies new challenges, and identity becomes invested in the relationship.
facts.commonError: A calling appears fully formed as an unmistakable inner revelation.
facts.whyWrong: The construct emphasizes developmental fit rather than instant discovery.

facts.claim: McAdams's personality model distinguishes dispositional traits, characteristic adaptations, and narrative identity.
facts.mechanism: Because Broad tendencies, context-bound goals, and life stories answer different questions about what a person is like.
facts.commonError: Personality is exhausted by a score on broad traits.
facts.whyWrong: Traits do not specify a person's projects, values, or story of who they are becoming.

facts.claim: Characteristic adaptations include goals, values, coping strategies, and relationship patterns shaped by context.
facts.mechanism: Because They translate broad traits into what a person is trying to do in a particular social world.
facts.commonError: Goals and values are fixed biological traits.
facts.whyWrong: They develop in cultural and life-stage contexts and can be revised more readily than broad temperament.

facts.claim: Durkheim's Suicide was published in 1897 and analyzed social integration and regulation.
facts.mechanism: Because Comparing population patterns allowed him to relate suicide rates to the strength and structure of social ties.
facts.commonError: Durkheim explained suicide only through individual mental illness.
facts.whyWrong: His distinctive contribution was a sociological account of patterned rates.

facts.claim: Anomie describes weakened or disrupted normative regulation rather than freedom in a purely positive sense.
facts.mechanism: Because When expectations and obligations lose structure, desires and social roles become harder to orient.
facts.commonError: Fewer social constraints always produce more meaningful autonomy.
facts.whyWrong: Some shared limits make commitment, trust, and legible roles possible.

facts.claim: Purpose within life can be investigated through a person's commitments even when a cosmic purpose cannot be empirically established.
facts.mechanism: Because Relationships, work, and institutions create observable patterns of significance, obligation, and identity.
facts.commonError: Meaning is impossible unless everyone accepts one metaphysical answer to why the universe exists.
facts.whyWrong: Practical meaning can arise from coherent commitments without resolving the cosmic question.
